raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old male farmer presented to our hospital complaining of waist pain and the left leg with lower limb weakness for the past 5 months. He reported weight loss of 5 kg, but no fever, cough, headache, dizziness, chills, night sweats, nausea, or vomiting. In local hospital, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine at that time showed bone destruction of the fourth lumbar vertebral body (L4) and left side appendages and the paravertebral soft tissue. Infection with abscess formation or bone tumor was tentatively diagnosed at the local hospital. He was transferred to our hospital for further management. The patient denied a history of exposure to pigeons.
On admission, physical examination revealed obvious tenderness with pain upon percussion over the spine on the fourth lumbar vertebra, muscle atrophy of left lower extremity, and the straight leg raising test (SLRT) was suspiciously positive. MRI of lumbar spine was performed, which displayed partial cortical bone destruction of L4 that involved spinal canal and intervertebral foramen causing secondary spinal canal stenosis at that level and cauda equina compression. A chest CT scan demonstrated small round nodules with uneven density of upper right lung (Figure 1). No abnormalities were seen on MRI scan of the brain. Initial bloodwork showed the following: leukocyte count of 6.72 (normal: 4-11) x 109/L, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 62 mm/h (normal: <20 mm/h). Cryptococcus capsular polysaccharide antigen was positive. 1,3-beta-D-Glucan detection and T-SPOT were negative. HbA1c was in the normal range. Tumor markers (including alpha fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, beta2-microglobulin, ferroprotein, and estradiol), antinuclear antibody, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, CD4 count, CD8 count, and serum complement were not obviously abnormal. Blood culture was negative. Patient had no diabetes mellitus, solid-organ transplantation, malignancy, and cirrhosis. In addition, vastus lateralis by percutaneous needle biopsy under local anesthesia percutaneous puncture on L4 spine was performed, and postoperative pathology showed fungal-like structure and infiltration with chronic inflammatory cells in the tissues submitted for examination (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry revealed CD68 (+), S100 (-), CK (-), KI67 15% (+). The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample was not obtained because our patient declined lumbar puncture. We first considered the diagnosis of cryptococcal infection with results of histopathological analysis and imaging examinations. Then we started empirical therapy with flucytosine plus amphotericin B. After five days, the plan was stopped, and switched to fluconazole at the dose of 400 mg per day because of impaired renal function.
Two weeks after his admission, the localized skin on the left lower back of the patient was slightly swollen with increased localized skin temperature. B-scan ultrasonography showed a 120 mm x 92 mm abnormal echo. Local abscess formation was considered. Then we performed percutaneous biopsy under ultrasound guidance. Pus culture was negative. The patient continued the treatment with the above-mentioned therapy, but his symptoms were not relieved. Ten days later, he had left lower extremity pain with hypoesthesia. Then he underwent surgical management by posterior lumbar open-window focal debridement. Postoperative pathology reported the following: periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) (+), Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) (+), CK (+), CD68(+), LCA (+), KI67 (+) (Figure 2). Cryptococcus neoformans var. grubii was confirmed from NGS data (Figure 3). The final diagnosis of disseminated vertebral cryptococcosis was made on the basis of the result of NGS combined with clinical manifestation, laboratory, imaging, and pathological findings. The patient continued treatment by fluconazole at the dose of 400 mg per day and was discharged, having made an improvement, 20 days after surgery. The patient's focal lesion was reduced, and the clinical symptoms disappeared at 12-month follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old male farmer presented with a 5-month history of lower back pain, left lower extremity weakness, and a 5-kg weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 5 months prior to admission, the patient developed progressive lumbar pain, left lower limb weakness, and a 5-kg weight loss without fever or respiratory/neurological symptoms. An outside lumbar MRI showed L4 vertebral and left paravertebral destruction suspicious for bone tumor or abscess, prompting transfer.
subjective.past_medical_history: No history of diabetes mellitus, organ transplantation, malignancy, cirrhosis, or known pigeon exposure; farmer by occupation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for lower back pain, left leg weakness (and subsequent left leg pain/hypoesthesia), and 5-kg weight loss. Negative for fever, cough, headache, dizziness, chills, night sweats, nausea, or vomiting.

objective.physical_examination: Marked percussion tenderness over the L4 spinous process, left lower extremity muscle atrophy, and a suspiciously positive straight-leg raising test; 2 weeks after admission, developed warm localized swelling over the left lower back and left lower extremity pain and hypoesthesia.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 6.72 x 10^9/L (normal: 4-11), elevated ESR 62 mm/h (normal: <20 mm/h), positive serum Cryptococcus capsular polysaccharide antigen, and negative 1,3-beta-D-glucan, T-SPOT.TB, blood cultures, HIV antibody, ANA, ANCA, and tumor markers (AFP, CEA, beta2-microglobulin, ferritin, estradiol), with normal HbA1c, CD4/CD8 counts, and serum complement.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar spine MRI demonstrated partial cortical bone destruction of the L4 vertebral body and left appendages involving the spinal canal and intervertebral foramen with secondary canal stenosis and cauda equina compression; B-scan ultrasound at week 2 showed a 120 x 92 mm left paraspinal abscess. Chest CT showed small round right upper lung nodules; brain MRI was normal (patient declined lumbar puncture). Initial percutaneous L4 needle biopsy and subsequent open posterior lumbar focal debridement histopathology showed chronic granulomatous inflammation with fungal structures positive on PAS and Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) stains (CD68+, LCA+, Ki-67 15%, S100-), and next-generation sequencing (NGS) confirmed Cryptococcus neoformans var. grubii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of disseminated L4 vertebral cryptococcal osteomyelitis (spondylitis) with paravertebral abscess, cauda equina compression, and pulmonary nodules caused by Cryptococcus neoformans var. grubii in an immunocompetent farmer, confirmed by positive serum cryptococcal capsular antigen, L4 biopsy/surgical pathology (PAS and GMS positive), and tissue next-generation sequencing. Initial amphotericin B plus flucytosine was switched after 5 days to oral fluconazole (400 mg/day) due to renal impairment; following progression of the paraspinal abscess and radicular pain, he underwent posterior lumbar open-window focal surgical debridement plus continued oral fluconazole (400 mg/day), discharging 20 days postoperatively with complete symptom resolution and lesion regression at 12-month follow-up.
